subject: English
summaryPoints: The subjunctive verb 'wish' expresses counterfactual or unfulfilled desires: wish + past simple/continuous indicates present unreality, wish + past perfect expresses retrospective past regret, and wish + would/could + bare infinitive denotes future desires or dissatisfaction with another's habit.
In formal English wish structures for the present, the subjunctive 'were' is used for all persons, including first and third-person singular (e.g., 'I wish I were taller').

Gerunds are verbal nouns ending in '-ing' that function syntactically in four core roles: as the subject of a verb, direct object of a transitive verb, object of a preposition, and subject complement following a linking verb.
Result clauses indicate consequences of actions or situations, introduced by coordinators and subordinators such as 'so', 'so...that', and 'such...that'.

Run-on sentences occur when two or more independent clauses are joined without appropriate punctuation or coordinating conjunctions, and can be repaired via: (1) a period separating two sentences, (2) a semicolon, or (3) a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).

Phrasal verbs are structurally classified into three grammatical types: separable transitive (verb + adverb + object), inseparable intransitive (verb + adverb, no object), and three-part inseparable transitive (verb + adverb + preposition + object).

formulas.label: Wish for Present Unreality (Subjunctive)
formulas.expr: Subject + wish + Subject + Simple Past (V2 / were)  [Expresses: action is currently not true]

formulas.label: Wish for Past Regret (Counterfactual Past)
formulas.expr: Subject + wish + Subject + had + V3(past participle)  [Expresses: sorrow over unalterable past event]

formulas.label: Wish for Future / Complaint Formula
formulas.expr: Subject + wish + Subject + would / could + V1(bare infinitive)  [Expresses: desire for change/cessation]

formulas.label: Run-on Sentence Correction Formulas
formulas.expr: Independent Clause . Independent Clause  OR  Independent Clause ; Independent Clause  OR  Independent Clause , + coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS) + Independent Clause

examTip: Never use 'will' or present tense verbs in a wish clause. A wish about the present requires the past tense (e.g., 'I wish I knew the answer', NOT 'know'). A wish expressing regret about the past requires the past perfect (e.g., 'I wish I had worked harder', NOT 'worked'). Also, avoid run-on comma splices: two complete independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.

keyDefinitions.definition: A syntactic construction used with past tense forms to articulate counterfactual desires, hypothetical situations, or past regrets that are contrary to fact.
A non-finite verb form ending in '-ing' that retains verb characteristics while functioning grammatically as a noun (subject, direct object, prepositional object, or complement).
A structural grammatical error occurring when two or more independent clauses are fused together without appropriate punctuation or coordinating conjunctions.
A subordinate adverbial clause introduced by conjunctions such as 'so', 'so...that', or 'such...that' that demonstrates the consequence or outcome of the matrix clause.
